question: Motion in a straight line is most closely described by which idea?
opt_a: Position changes with time along any path
opt_b: Position changes with time on a straight line
opt_c: Velocity changes with time without a path
opt_d: Distance from origin is recorded at one instant
explanation: Motion means that the position of a body changes with time. For motion in a straight line, the position is restricted to one chosen line, so a single coordinate is enough to describe where the body is located. Examples include a lift moving vertically, a train moving along a straight track, or a runner moving along a straight lane. A single distance reading, a velocity change, or an unspecified path does not by itself give the one-dimensional idea of motion unless position changes with time along the chosen straight line. The phrase “with time” is essential because motion compares positions at different instants.

question: A lift moves from the ground floor to the third floor and then stops. Why is this a suitable example of one-dimensional motion?
explanation: One-dimensional motion means motion that can be described along a single straight line. A lift moves up or down along the same vertical line, so its position can be represented by one coordinate on that line. The motion may be fast, slow, uniform, or non-uniform; constant speed is not required for one-dimensional motion. Stopping only means the position is not changing at that instant, not that the whole displacement must be zero. The important feature is the line of motion, not whether the object is moving at a constant rate.

question: To record the position of a train on a straight track, a fixed station \(O\) is chosen as \(x=0\). What role does \(O\) play in this description?
opt_a: The point where speed is measured
opt_b: The point where acceleration is zero
opt_d: The reference for total path length
explanation: A position coordinate needs a starting point from which positions are measured. The fixed station \(O\) acts as the origin, so the coordinate \(x\) of the train is measured relative to that point. Without an origin, a statement such as \(x=200\,\text{m}\) would not tell us where the train is located. The origin is not a speed, acceleration, or distance travelled; it is part of the coordinate description. Choosing a different origin changes the numerical coordinate, but it does not move the train physically.

question: On a straight road, east is chosen as the positive direction. A bicycle is moving west. How should the direction of its motion be represented in this coordinate description?
opt_a: By positive velocity along the chosen axis
opt_b: By negative velocity along the chosen axis
opt_c: By zero velocity on the chosen axis
opt_d: By speed only, with no direction sign
explanation: In one-dimensional motion, a positive direction is chosen first. If east is positive, then motion toward west is in the negative direction. The negative sign does not mean that the bicycle has no motion or that its speed is negative. It only gives direction relative to the chosen axis. The unit \( \text{m s}^{-1} \) still describes velocity, while the sign tells whether the motion is along or opposite to the positive direction.

question:
Match the basic kinematic symbols with their usual meanings.
SymbolMeaning
P. \(x\)1. Time
Q. \(t\)2. Acceleration
R. \(v\)3. Position coordinate
S. \(a\)4. Velocity
explanation: The symbol \(x\) commonly denotes the position coordinate of a body on the chosen line. The symbol \(t\) denotes time, while \(v\) denotes velocity and \(a\) denotes acceleration. These symbols help write compact relations later, such as velocity being related to change of position with time. Confusing \(x\) with distance or \(a\) with speed can lead to wrong formula use in later parts of the chapter. The symbols are meaningful only after the coordinate axis and time measurement have been fixed.

question: The SI unit of acceleration is ______.
explanation: Acceleration describes how velocity changes per unit time. Since velocity has SI unit \( \text{m s}^{-1} \), dividing it by time in \( \text{s} \) gives \( \text{m s}^{-2} \). The unit \( \text{m} \) belongs to position, distance, or displacement, not acceleration. The unit \( \text{m s}^{-1} \) belongs to speed or velocity. The exponent \(-2\) on \( \text{s} \) shows that time appears twice in the denominator when acceleration is expressed in SI units.

question: A runner stays in one straight lane while moving from one end of the track to the other. What makes the motion suitable for description by a single coordinate \(x\)?
opt_a: Position changes along one chosen line
opt_b: Speed remains constant in the same lane
opt_c: The runner returns to the starting point
opt_d: Displacement is zero in each interval
explanation: A single coordinate \(x\) is enough when the motion is along one straight line. The runner’s changing position can then be marked by different values of \(x\) on that line. The runner’s mass, shoes, or style of running are not the reason for using one-dimensional kinematics. Returning to the starting point is also not required; a runner may move only forward and still have one-dimensional motion. The coordinate idea depends on the geometry of the path used for description.

question: A box is lying on the floor of a bus moving uniformly along a straight road. For a passenger sitting inside the bus, how is the box best described?
opt_a: At rest relative to the passenger
opt_b: Moving backward relative to the passenger
opt_c: Accelerating upward relative to the passenger
opt_d: Moving forward relative to the bus floor
explanation: Rest and motion depend on the frame of reference. The box and the passenger are moving together with the bus, so the position of the box relative to the passenger does not change. For a person standing on the road, the same box is moving along with the bus. This does not create a contradiction because the two observers are using different frames. A body can be at rest in one frame and in motion in another frame at the same time.

question: A lamp post is fixed beside a road. A car passes it and moves away. In the frame of the road, what changes with time for the car?
opt_a: Its speed unit relative to the road
opt_b: The time reading of one second
opt_c: Its position relative to the lamp post
opt_d: The origin chosen by the road observer
explanation: In the road frame, the lamp post can be treated as a fixed reference object. As the car moves away, its position relative to the lamp post changes with time. That change of position is the basic kinematic description of motion. The unit of mass and the value of time do not change because the car moves. The origin is chosen by the observer; it does not shift automatically just because the car passes a point.

question: A straight corridor is marked with an origin \(O\), and the positive direction is to the right. A point \(P\) is \(3\,\text{m}\) to the left of \(O\). What coordinate should be assigned to \(P\)?
explanation: The coordinate sign is decided by the chosen positive direction. Since the positive direction is to the right, points to the left of the origin have negative coordinates. The point is \(3\,\text{m}\) from \(O\), so its coordinate is \(-3\,\text{m}\). The sign is part of the coordinate description, while the number \(3\,\text{m}\) tells how far the point is from the origin. A negative coordinate does not mean a negative physical length; it means the point lies on the negative side of the axis.

question:
Assertion: Rest and motion are relative terms.
Reason: The description of rest or motion can depend on the observer’s frame of reference.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: A body is said to be at rest if its position does not change with time in a chosen frame of reference. The same body is said to be in motion if its position changes with time in another frame. For example, a seated passenger is at rest relative to the bus but moving relative to the road. This shows that rest and motion are not absolute descriptions in ordinary kinematics. The Reason gives the exact basis for the Assertion because the observer’s frame decides the position measurement.

question: Changing the origin from one end of a straight track to the middle of the track will most directly change which description of a runner?
opt_a: The runner’s physical location on the track
opt_d: The runner’s time interval of motion
explanation: The physical location of the runner does not change merely because a new origin is chosen. However, the numerical coordinate \(x\) depends on where \(x=0\) is placed. If the origin is shifted, the same point on the track may receive a different coordinate value. This is why position coordinates are always stated relative to an origin and an axis direction. The choice of origin changes the description, not the actual place occupied by the runner.

question: A motion record uses \( \text{m} \), \( \text{s} \), \( \text{m s}^{-1} \), and \( \text{m s}^{-2} \). Which pairing is most suitable for basic one-dimensional kinematics?
explanation: Position coordinate \(x\) is a length-type quantity, so its SI unit is \( \text{m} \). Time \(t\) is measured in \( \text{s} \). Velocity \(v\) is change of position per unit time, so its unit is \( \text{m s}^{-1} \). Acceleration \(a\) is change of velocity per unit time, so its unit is \( \text{m s}^{-2} \). Unit pairing is not just memory work; it also helps detect whether a later formula has the right physical meaning.

question: In a straight-line description, two observers choose opposite positive directions along the same road. A cyclist is moving toward the east. What can happen to the sign of the cyclist’s velocity in their descriptions?
opt_c: Opposite signs in the two descriptions
opt_d: Zero in one description and non-zero in the other
explanation: The sign of velocity depends on the chosen positive direction. If one observer chooses east as positive, the eastward velocity is positive in that coordinate system. If another observer chooses west as positive, the same eastward velocity is negative in that coordinate system. The cyclist’s actual motion does not stop or change because the sign convention changes. A sign convention is a language for describing direction, not a force acting on the moving body.

question: Use the arrangement described below. A straight line has origin \(O\). Point \(L\) is \(5\,\text{m}\) to the left of \(O\), and point \(R\) is \(5\,\text{m}\) to the right of \(O\). The positive direction is chosen toward the right. What is the best coordinate description of the two points?
explanation: The origin \(O\) is the zero point for position coordinates. Since the positive direction is toward the right, the point on the right has a positive coordinate and the point on the left has a negative coordinate. Both points are equally far from the origin, so the magnitudes of their coordinates are the same. The signs differ because the points lie on opposite sides of \(O\). The coordinate sign tells side of the origin, while the magnitude tells separation from the origin.

question: A person walking inside a train says, “I am moving forward.” A person standing on the platform also sees the train moving forward. Why is a frame of reference still needed to describe the person’s motion clearly?
opt_a: Because positions are measured in a chosen frame
opt_b: Because the train frame must use a different unit
opt_c: Because acceleration must be zero in every frame
opt_d: Because the platform observer cannot measure position
explanation: A frame of reference tells us from where position is being measured. The person’s motion relative to the train may differ from the person’s motion relative to the platform. If the person walks forward inside a train that is also moving forward, the platform frame and train frame may assign different speeds and positions. The need for a frame does not mean the train frame needs a different unit or that motion must have zero acceleration. The unit \( \text{m} \) remains the same, but the coordinate description depends on the chosen reference frame.

question: A phone kept on a seat in a moving train is observed by two people: one sitting beside it in the train and one standing on the platform. The most complete description is that the phone is
opt_a: at rest in every frame because it does not slide
opt_b: moving in every frame because the train is moving
opt_c: at rest in train frame and moving in platform frame
opt_d: neither at rest nor in motion because observers disagree
explanation: Rest and motion are decided by checking whether position changes with time in a chosen frame of reference. For the passenger sitting beside the phone, the phone’s position relative to the seat remains unchanged, so it is at rest in the train frame. For the person on the platform, the phone moves along with the train, so its position changes with time in the platform frame. The two descriptions are not contradictory because they belong to different reference frames. A clear kinematic statement should mention or imply the frame in which the position is being measured.

question: A straight road is described using a coordinate axis. The town gate is first chosen as origin \(O\), but later a milestone \(2\,\text{km}\) east of the gate is chosen as the new origin. What remains unchanged by this new choice?
opt_a: The physical location of a parked car on the road
opt_b: The coordinate \(x\) of every point on the road
opt_c: The sign of every coordinate on the road
opt_d: The numerical value of the car’s position coordinate
explanation: Changing the origin changes the coordinate description, not the actual location of objects. A parked car remains at the same physical point on the road whether the origin is the town gate or the milestone. Its coordinate \(x\) may change because position is measured from a different zero point. The sign of the coordinate may also change if the new origin lies on the other side of the car. Coordinates are part of a chosen description, while the physical location is not altered by relabelling the axis.

question: In a one-dimensional record, a cart has coordinate \(x=-6\,\text{m}\) at one instant. This statement by itself tells us that the cart is
opt_b: located at the origin after moving \(6\,\text{m}\)
opt_d: accelerating toward the negative side of the axis
explanation: A negative position coordinate tells where the body is relative to the chosen origin and positive direction. The coordinate \(x=-6\,\text{m}\) means the cart is \(6\,\text{m}\) from the origin on the negative side of the axis. It does not tell whether the cart is moving, at rest, speeding up, or slowing down. Direction of motion needs information about how position changes with time, not just one position value. A coordinate sign should not be confused with the sign of velocity.

question:
Study the position records of a toy car on a straight line.
TimePosition coordinate
\(t=0\,\text{s}\)\(x=+2\,\text{m}\)
\(t=1\,\text{s}\)\(x=+2\,\text{m}\)
\(t=2\,\text{s}\)\(x=+2\,\text{m}\)
What does the table show in the chosen frame?
opt_a: The car is at rest at \(x=+2\,\text{m}\)
opt_b: The car is moving in the positive direction
opt_c: The car is moving in the negative direction
opt_d: The car has zero velocity at \(x=+2\,\text{m}\)
explanation: In a given frame, a body is at rest when its position coordinate does not change with time. Here the coordinate remains \(x=+2\,\text{m}\) at \(t=0\,\text{s}\), \(t=1\,\text{s}\), and \(t=2\,\text{s}\). The positive coordinate only tells that the car is on the positive side of the origin. It does not mean the car is moving in the positive direction. A constant position coordinate represents rest in that chosen frame.

question: Two coordinate descriptions are made for the same straight path. Case 1: east is positive. Case 2: west is positive. A scooter moves \(4\,\text{m}\) east from a point. How is this displacement represented in the two cases?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given direction:} \) The scooter moves \(4\,\text{m}\) east.
\( \textbf{Case 1 convention:} \) East is chosen as positive.
So the eastward displacement is written as \(+4\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Case 2 convention:} \) West is chosen as positive.
East is now opposite to the positive direction, so the same displacement is written as \(-4\,\text{m}\).
The physical motion is unchanged in both cases.
Only the sign used in the coordinate description changes.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The displacement is \(+4\,\text{m}\) in Case 1 and \(-4\,\text{m}\) in Case 2.

question:
Consider the following statements about a one-dimensional coordinate system.
Statement I: The origin fixes the point from which position is measured.
Statement II: The positive direction fixes the sign convention on the line.
Statement III: A negative coordinate always means the object is moving backward.
explanation: The origin is the point labelled \(x=0\), so it fixes the reference point for measuring position. The chosen positive direction decides which side of the origin receives positive coordinate values. A negative coordinate only shows that the object is on the negative side of the origin. It does not by itself show the direction of motion. To decide whether the object is moving backward or forward, positions at different instants or the sign of velocity must be known.

question: A bus moves along a straight road, while a passenger walks from the rear of the bus toward the front. The phrase “the passenger moves forward” is incomplete in physics unless it also makes clear
opt_a: the road’s chosen origin for coordinates
opt_b: the frame or reference used for motion
opt_c: the coordinate sign assigned to the bus
opt_d: the time interval for the passenger’s walk
explanation: A direction such as “forward” must be understood relative to a chosen frame or reference direction. The passenger may be moving toward the front of the bus relative to the bus, while the motion relative to the ground depends on the bus’s own motion. Kinematics describes position changes relative to a reference frame, so the frame is not a decorative detail. The road origin, bus coordinate sign, and route length do not by themselves decide the meaning of the motion description. A complete description of motion must connect the position change with the observer or coordinate system used.

question: A bead is constrained to move along a straight wire. The wire itself is bent neither upward nor sideways in the chosen description. Why can the bead’s motion be treated as one-dimensional?
opt_a: The bead can be located by a single coordinate along the wire
opt_b: The bead must have zero acceleration at every instant
opt_c: The bead must move with equal displacements in equal times
opt_d: The bead’s distance and displacement must always have the same value
explanation: Motion is one-dimensional when the position of the body can be specified by one coordinate along a line. A bead constrained to a straight wire has no independent sideways coordinate in the chosen description. This does not require uniform motion or zero acceleration. The bead may speed up, slow down, or reverse direction while still remaining on the same straight line. Distance and displacement become equal only under special motion without reversal, not merely because the motion is one-dimensional.

question: A runner is at \(x=-8\,\text{m}\) at \(t=0\,\text{s}\) and at \(x=-3\,\text{m}\) at \(t=2\,\text{s}\). What can be concluded from these coordinates?
opt_a: The runner has moved toward the positive direction
opt_b: The runner has moved toward the negative direction
opt_c: The runner must be at the origin during the interval
opt_d: The runner has remained at rest
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial position:} \) \(x_1=-8\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final position:} \) \(x_2=-3\,\text{m}\).
The coordinate has increased from \(-8\,\text{m}\) to \(-3\,\text{m}\).
An increase in \(x\) means motion toward the positive direction on the chosen axis.
The runner is still on the negative side of the origin at \(x=-3\,\text{m}\), but the direction of change is positive.
The runner does not need to cross \(x=0\) to move in the positive direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The runner has moved toward the positive direction.

question: A coordinate \(x=+12\,\text{m}\) is assigned to a stone at a certain instant. The most precise meaning of this record is that the stone is
explanation: The coordinate \(x=+12\,\text{m}\) is a position record, not a speed or acceleration record. It means the stone is \(12\,\text{m}\) from the origin on the positive side of the chosen axis. The unit \( \text{m} \) confirms that the quantity is length-type. Velocity would require a unit such as \( \text{m s}^{-1} \), and acceleration would require \( \text{m s}^{-2} \). The coordinate is measured from the selected origin, not from every possible observer in space.

question: A student writes the following line in a notebook: “Since \(x=-5\,\text{m}\), the body must be moving left.” What is the flaw in this reasoning?
opt_a: Position sign has no SI unit
explanation: The value \(x=-5\,\text{m}\) describes where the body is located relative to the chosen origin. It places the body on the negative side of the coordinate axis. Direction of motion requires information about change in position with time, such as whether \(x\) is increasing or decreasing. The body at \(x=-5\,\text{m}\) could be moving left, moving right, or momentarily at rest. Position sign and velocity sign are related ideas, but they are not the same information.

question: Use the arrangement described below. A straight line has marks at \(x=-4\,\text{m}\), \(x=0\,\text{m}\), \(x=+3\,\text{m}\), and \(x=+7\,\text{m}\). A marble is first at \(x=+3\,\text{m}\) and later at \(x=+7\,\text{m}\). What feature of the coordinate record shows the marble moved in the positive direction?
opt_a: Both positions are on the positive side
opt_b: The coordinate value increases with time
opt_c: The origin lies between two marked positions
explanation: Direction of motion in one dimension is decided by how the coordinate changes with time. The marble moves from \(x=+3\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+7\,\text{m}\), so the value of \(x\) increases. Increasing \(x\) means motion in the chosen positive direction. The fact that both coordinates are positive only tells that both positions are on the positive side of the origin. The unit is \( \text{m} \) for both positions, so the direction comes from coordinate change, not from any change in unit.

question:
A table records positions of three objects on the same straight line at one instant.
ObjectPosition coordinate
P\(-2\,\text{m}\)
Q\(+5\,\text{m}\)
R\(0\,\text{m}\)
The row interpretation that matches the coordinate system is
opt_a: P is on the negative side, Q is on the positive side, and R is at the origin
opt_b: P has negative velocity, Q has positive velocity, and R has zero velocity
opt_c: P has negative displacement, Q has positive displacement, and R has zero distance
opt_d: P is moving left, Q is moving right, and R is accelerating
explanation: A position coordinate tells location relative to the chosen origin and direction. Object P has \(x=-2\,\text{m}\), so it lies on the negative side of the origin. Object Q has \(x=+5\,\text{m}\), so it lies on the positive side. Object R has \(x=0\,\text{m}\), so it is at the origin itself. The table gives only positions at one instant, so it cannot decide speeds, velocities, or acceleration.

question: At \(t=0\,\text{s}\), a cart is at \(x=+6\,\text{m}\). At \(t=4\,\text{s}\), it is at \(x=+1\,\text{m}\). What is the simplest direction information from this position record?
opt_a: The cart moved in the positive direction
opt_b: The cart moved in the negative direction
opt_c: The cart stayed at rest on the positive side
opt_d: The cart crossed the origin exactly once
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial position:} \) \(x_1=+6\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final position:} \) \(x_2=+1\,\text{m}\).
The coordinate decreases from \(+6\,\text{m}\) to \(+1\,\text{m}\).
A decrease in \(x\) means the motion is toward the negative direction.
The cart remains on the positive side at the final instant, but the direction of change is negative.
The data do not prove that the cart crossed the origin; both given coordinates are positive.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The cart moved in the negative direction during the recorded interval.

question:
Read the short record below.
A straight track has a fixed origin \(O\). A trolley is observed at \(x=-1\,\text{m}\) at \(t=0\,\text{s}\), at \(x=0\,\text{m}\) at \(t=1\,\text{s}\), and at \(x=+1\,\text{m}\) at \(t=2\,\text{s}\).
What does this record show about the trolley’s position?
opt_a: It moves from the negative side to the positive side through the origin
opt_b: It remains at the origin during the whole observation
opt_c: It moves from the positive side to the negative side through the origin
opt_d: It has zero position at every instant
explanation: The coordinate \(x=-1\,\text{m}\) places the trolley on the negative side of the origin at \(t=0\,\text{s}\). At \(t=1\,\text{s}\), the coordinate becomes \(x=0\,\text{m}\), so the trolley is at the origin. At \(t=2\,\text{s}\), the coordinate is \(x=+1\,\text{m}\), placing it on the positive side. The coordinate values increase with time, showing motion in the positive direction during this record. The origin is crossed because the table explicitly includes the instant where \(x=0\,\text{m}\).

question: The quantity \(x\) in a one-dimensional position-time record is best treated as
opt_a: a location relative to the chosen origin
opt_b: the total path length from the beginning
opt_c: the speed of the body at an instant
explanation: In straight-line kinematics, \(x\) usually denotes the position coordinate of the body. It tells where the body is relative to the origin and the chosen positive direction. It is not automatically the total path length covered because a body may move back and forth while having the same coordinate at different times. It is also not speed, since speed involves distance covered per unit time. Keeping position coordinate separate from path length is necessary before learning distance and displacement.

question: A body is at \(x=-3\,\text{m}\) at one instant and later at \(x=-9\,\text{m}\). The coordinate sign at both instants is negative, but the motion during the interval is best described as
opt_a: toward the positive direction because both coordinates are negative
opt_b: toward the negative direction because the coordinate decreases
opt_c: impossible because a coordinate cannot become more negative
opt_d: zero because both coordinates have the same sign
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial coordinate:} \) \(x_1=-3\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Later coordinate:} \) \(x_2=-9\,\text{m}\).
The value of \(x\) changes from \(-3\,\text{m}\) to \(-9\,\text{m}\), so it decreases.
In one-dimensional coordinate language, decreasing \(x\) indicates motion toward the negative direction.
The fact that both positions are negative only tells which side of the origin the body occupies.
Motion is decided from the change in coordinate, not from the sign of a single coordinate alone.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The motion is toward the negative direction.

question: A coordinate record gives \(x=0\,\text{m}\) for a box at \(t=5\,\text{s}\). This necessarily means that the box
explanation: The coordinate \(x=0\,\text{m}\) means the body is located at the origin of the chosen coordinate system at that instant. It does not say how the body reached that point. The box may have travelled some distance before arriving at the origin. It may also be moving through the origin or momentarily at rest there; the single position record does not decide velocity. Acceleration also cannot be concluded from one coordinate value alone because acceleration depends on how velocity changes with time.

question: In straight-line motion with possible reversal, distance travelled means
opt_a: the algebraic difference between final and initial coordinates
opt_b: the total length of the actual path covered
opt_c: the final position coordinate of the moving body
opt_d: the shortest signed change in position
explanation: Distance travelled is the total path length covered by a moving body. It is found by adding the lengths of all parts of the journey, even if the body reverses direction. Distance does not carry a positive or negative sign because it is a scalar quantity. The algebraic difference between final and initial coordinates is displacement, not distance. In back-and-forth motion, distance keeps increasing with every part of the path that is actually covered.

question: A child walks \(4\,\text{m}\) east and then \(3\,\text{m}\) west along the same straight path. What is the distance travelled?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given path:} \) The child first walks \(4\,\text{m}\) east and then \(3\,\text{m}\) west.
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Distance travelled.
Distance is the total path length, so directions are not subtracted.
\[
\text{Distance}=4\,\text{m}+3\,\text{m}
\]
\[
\text{Distance}=7\,\text{m}
\]
The westward part still contributes positively to distance because the child actually covers that length.
A result such as \(1\,\text{m}\) would describe the net change in position, not the total path covered.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The distance travelled is \(7\,\text{m}\).

question: A cart moves from \(x=+2\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+9\,\text{m}\) without reversing direction. The distance travelled during this part is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial coordinate:} \) \(x_1=+2\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final coordinate:} \) \(x_2=+9\,\text{m}\).
The motion is along one direction without reversal, so the path length equals the change in coordinate magnitude.
\[
\text{Distance}=9\,\text{m}-2\,\text{m}
\]
\[
\text{Distance}=7\,\text{m}
\]
The signs of the coordinates locate the points relative to the origin.
For this no-reversal part, the length of the covered path is simply the separation between the two positions.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The distance travelled is \(7\,\text{m}\).

question: A body goes from \(x=-5\,\text{m}\) to \(x=-1\,\text{m}\), and then returns to \(x=-4\,\text{m}\). What is its total distance travelled?
explanation:
\( \textbf{First part:} \) From \(x=-5\,\text{m}\) to \(x=-1\,\text{m}\).
\[
\text{Length of first part}=|-1-(-5)|\,\text{m}
\]
\[
\text{Length of first part}=4\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Second part:} \) From \(x=-1\,\text{m}\) to \(x=-4\,\text{m}\).
\[
\text{Length of second part}=|-4-(-1)|\,\text{m}
\]
\[
\text{Length of second part}=3\,\text{m}
\]
Distance is the sum of path lengths, not the algebraic change in coordinate.
\[
\text{Total distance}=4\,\text{m}+3\,\text{m}=7\,\text{m}
\]
The reversal must be counted as an additional covered length.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The total distance travelled is \(7\,\text{m}\).

question:
Study the record of a bead moving along a straight wire.
StagePosition on wire
Start\(x=0\,\text{m}\)
Next\(x=+6\,\text{m}\)
Final\(x=+2\,\text{m}\)
The distance travelled by the bead is
explanation:
\( \textbf{First segment:} \) The bead moves from \(x=0\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+6\,\text{m}\), so it covers \(6\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Second segment:} \) It then moves from \(x=+6\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+2\,\text{m}\), so it covers \(4\,\text{m}\).
The second motion is a reversal, but distance still counts the path length covered.
\[
\text{Total distance}=6\,\text{m}+4\,\text{m}
\]
\[
\text{Total distance}=10\,\text{m}
\]
The final coordinate \(+2\,\text{m}\) does not by itself represent the total distance covered.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The distance travelled is \(10\,\text{m}\).

question: The distance travelled by a moving body can never be negative because it is
opt_a: a scalar measure of total path length
opt_b: always equal to the final coordinate
opt_c: a signed vector-like change in position
opt_d: measured only when the body moves in the positive direction
explanation: Distance measures how much path length has been covered. A path length is counted as a non-negative quantity, regardless of whether motion is toward the positive or negative direction. The body may move left, right, up, or down along a line, but each covered segment adds positively to distance. Distance is not the same as final position coordinate because a coordinate can be positive, negative, or zero. The absence of sign in distance is what separates it from displacement in one-dimensional motion.

question:
Match the descriptions with the appropriate quantity.
DescriptionQuantity
P. Total length of path covered1. Position coordinate
Q. Location relative to origin2. Distance travelled
R. SI unit used for path length3. \( \text{m} \)
S. Quantity that cannot be negative4. Distance in ordinary kinematics
explanation: The total length of the path covered is distance travelled. A location relative to an origin is described by a position coordinate such as \(x\). The SI unit used for path length is \( \text{m} \). In ordinary kinematics, distance is non-negative because it counts covered length. The match separates location from path length, which is necessary when the same final position can be reached through different paths.

question:
Read the situation below.
A person walks from a gate to a shop \(120\,\text{m}\) away along a straight road. After buying a notebook, the person walks \(40\,\text{m}\) back toward the gate.
What distance has the person travelled?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Outward walk:} \) The person covers \(120\,\text{m}\) from the gate to the shop.
\( \textbf{Return part:} \) The person then covers \(40\,\text{m}\) back toward the gate.
Distance adds the actual lengths of all parts of the walk.
\[
\text{Total distance}=120\,\text{m}+40\,\text{m}
\]
\[
\text{Total distance}=160\,\text{m}
\]
The return direction does not make the \(40\,\text{m}\) negative for distance.
Subtracting would give the net change from the gate, not the full path length walked.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The distance travelled is \(160\,\text{m}\).

question: A distance record for a moving ant says \(15\,\text{cm}\). In SI units, this distance is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Distance \(=15\,\text{cm}\).
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Distance in SI unit \( \text{m} \).
The conversion relation is
\[
1\,\text{cm}=10^{-2}\,\text{m}
\]
So,
\[
15\,\text{cm}=15\times10^{-2}\,\text{m}
\]
\[
15\,\text{cm}=0.15\,\text{m}
\]
Distance remains a non-negative length during unit conversion.
The numerical value changes because \( \text{m} \) is a larger unit than \( \text{cm} \).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The SI value is \(0.15\,\text{m}\).

question: Displacement in one-dimensional motion is best defined as
opt_a: total length of the actual path covered
opt_b: change from initial to final coordinate
opt_c: distance covered only in the positive direction
opt_d: final coordinate divided by total time
explanation: Displacement describes how much the position changes from the initial point to the final point. In one-dimensional motion, it is written as \( \Delta x=x_2-x_1 \). The sign of \( \Delta x \) shows whether the net change is toward the positive or negative direction. It does not add every segment of the actual path; that is the role of distance. This is why displacement can be positive, negative, or zero, while distance cannot be negative.

question: A toy car moves from \(x=-2\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+5\,\text{m}\). Its displacement is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial position:} \) \(x_1=-2\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final position:} \) \(x_2=+5\,\text{m}\).
Displacement in one dimension is
\[
\Delta x=x_2-x_1
\]
Substituting the values,
\[
\Delta x=+5\,\text{m}-(-2\,\text{m})
\]
\[
\Delta x=+5\,\text{m}+2\,\text{m}
\]
\[
\Delta x=+7\,\text{m}
\]
The positive sign means the net change in position is toward the positive direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The displacement is \(+7\,\text{m}\).

question: A motion starts at \(x=+10\,\text{m}\) and ends at \(x=+4\,\text{m}\). What does the displacement show?
opt_a: \(+6\,\text{m}\), net change toward the positive direction
opt_b: \(-6\,\text{m}\), net change toward the negative direction
opt_c: \(+14\,\text{m}\), total length from origin to final point
opt_d: \(-14\,\text{m}\), total distance from origin to start point
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial coordinate:} \) \(x_1=+10\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final coordinate:} \) \(x_2=+4\,\text{m}\).
Use the displacement relation
\[
\Delta x=x_2-x_1
\]
\[
\Delta x=+4\,\text{m}-(+10\,\text{m})
\]
\[
\Delta x=-6\,\text{m}
\]
The negative sign means the final position is \(6\,\text{m}\) toward the negative side from the initial position.
Both coordinates are positive, but the change in coordinate is negative.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The displacement is \(-6\,\text{m}\), toward the negative direction.

question: A body travels from \(x=0\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+8\,\text{m}\), then returns to \(x=0\,\text{m}\). What is its displacement for the complete motion?
explanation:
Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions. Here the body starts at \(x=0\,\text{m}\) and also ends at \(x=0\,\text{m}\). Therefore,
\[
\Delta x=x_2-x_1=0\,\text{m}-0\,\text{m}
\]
\[
\Delta x=0\,\text{m}
\]
The body has certainly covered a path, but the net change in position is zero. Returning to the starting point makes displacement zero even when the distance travelled is not zero.

question: A displacement of \(-12\,\text{m}\) along a chosen \(x\)-axis means that
opt_a: a distance of \(-12\,\text{m}\) has been covered
explanation: A displacement sign gives the direction of the net change in position. The value \(-12\,\text{m}\) means the final position is \(12\,\text{m}\) toward the negative direction from the initial position. It does not mean the distance travelled is negative, because distance is never negative. It also does not necessarily mean the final coordinate is \(x=-12\,\text{m}\); that would depend on the initial coordinate. The unit \( \text{m} \) indicates displacement, not speed.

question:
Two motions along the same straight line are described below.
Motion P: \(x=+1\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+6\,\text{m}\)
Motion Q: \(x=-4\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+1\,\text{m}\)
What is true about their displacements?
opt_a: P has larger displacement than Q
opt_b: Q has larger displacement than P
explanation:
\( \textbf{Motion P:} \)
\[
\Delta x_P=+6\,\text{m}-(+1\,\text{m})=+5\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Motion Q:} \)
\[
\Delta x_Q=+1\,\text{m}-(-4\,\text{m})=+5\,\text{m}
\]
Both final coordinates are \(5\,\text{m}\) greater than their initial coordinates.
The starting positions are different, but the net change in coordinate is the same.
The positive sign shows that both displacements are toward the positive direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Both motions have displacement \(+5\,\text{m}\).

question:
Consider the following statements about displacement in one-dimensional motion.
Statement I: Displacement can be zero even when distance travelled is not zero.
Statement II: Displacement is calculated using \( \Delta x=x_2-x_1 \).
Statement III: Displacement must always be positive because it is measured in \( \text{m} \).
explanation: Statement I is true because a body may return to its starting point after covering some path, giving zero displacement but non-zero distance. Statement II is true because displacement in one-dimensional motion is the change in position, \( \Delta x=x_2-x_1 \). Statement III is false because displacement is a signed quantity in one dimension. Its unit \( \text{m} \) does not force it to be positive. The sign of displacement comes from coordinate change, not from the unit used.

question: A person moves along a straight path from \(x=-6\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+2\,\text{m}\), then to \(x=-1\,\text{m}\). The displacement for the full motion is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial position:} \) \(x_1=-6\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final position:} \) \(x_2=-1\,\text{m}\).
For displacement, only the initial and final positions are needed.
\[
\Delta x=x_2-x_1
\]
\[
\Delta x=-1\,\text{m}-(-6\,\text{m})
\]
\[
\Delta x=+5\,\text{m}
\]
The intermediate visit to \(x=+2\,\text{m}\) affects distance travelled, but not the displacement formula.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The displacement for the full motion is \(+5\,\text{m}\).

question:
A data sheet gives the following position-time entries for a moving object.
InstantPosition coordinate
\(t_1\)\(-3\,\text{m}\)
\(t_2\)\(+4\,\text{m}\)
\(t_3\)\(+1\,\text{m}\)
The displacement from \(t_1\) to \(t_3\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial instant:} \) At \(t_1\), \(x_1=-3\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final instant:} \) At \(t_3\), \(x_2=+1\,\text{m}\).
The entry at \(t_2\) is an intermediate position and is not used directly for displacement from \(t_1\) to \(t_3\).
\[
\Delta x=x_2-x_1
\]
\[
\Delta x=+1\,\text{m}-(-3\,\text{m})
\]
\[
\Delta x=+4\,\text{m}
\]
The positive sign shows that the final position is \(4\,\text{m}\) toward the positive direction from the initial position.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The displacement from \(t_1\) to \(t_3\) is \(+4\,\text{m}\).

question: For any motion along a straight line, the relation between distance travelled and magnitude of displacement is
opt_b: \(\text{distance}\lt|\Delta x|\) whenever the body reverses direction
opt_d: \(\text{distance}=-|\Delta x|\) if motion is in the negative direction
explanation: Distance is the total length of the actual path covered, while \(|\Delta x|\) is the magnitude of the net change in position. If a body moves directly from the initial point to the final point without reversing direction, the total path length equals the magnitude of displacement. If the body reverses direction, extra path length is added while the net separation between initial and final positions may remain smaller. This is why distance can be greater than displacement magnitude, but not less than it. The sign of displacement is removed in \(|\Delta x|\), so comparison with distance is made between non-negative quantities.

question: A body moves from \(x=0\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+5\,\text{m}\), then comes back to \(x=+2\,\text{m}\). The distance travelled and magnitude of displacement are respectively
explanation:
\( \textbf{Path segments:} \) The body first moves from \(x=0\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+5\,\text{m}\), covering \(5\,\text{m}\).
It then moves back from \(x=+5\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+2\,\text{m}\), covering \(3\,\text{m}\).
Distance is the sum of covered path lengths:
\[
\text{distance}=5\,\text{m}+3\,\text{m}=7\,\text{m}
\]
For displacement, use only initial and final positions:
\[
\Delta x=x_2-x_1=+2\,\text{m}-0\,\text{m}=+2\,\text{m}
\]
So the magnitude of displacement is
\[
|\Delta x|=2\,\text{m}
\]
The return part increases distance but reduces the net change in position.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Distance \(=7\,\text{m}\), and \(|\Delta x|=2\,\text{m}\).

question: Equality between distance travelled and magnitude of displacement is possible when a body
opt_a: moves along a straight line without reversing direction
opt_b: starts and ends at the same position
opt_c: changes direction at least once during the motion
opt_d: moves in the negative direction only after returning to the origin
explanation: Distance counts the total path length covered, while displacement magnitude measures the straight separation between initial and final positions. In one-dimensional motion, these two become equal when the body moves from the initial point to the final point without reversing direction. Once a reversal occurs, some part of the path is retraced or added, making distance larger than the magnitude of displacement. Starting and ending at the same position gives zero displacement, but the distance may be non-zero. Motion in the negative direction can still give equality if it is in one direction without reversal.

question: A runner makes an out-and-back run on a straight track segment by starting at a marker, running to another marker \(50\,\text{m}\) away, and returning to the starting marker. The distance and displacement for the complete motion are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Outward path:} \) The runner covers \(50\,\text{m}\) away from the starting marker.
\( \textbf{Return path:} \) The runner covers another \(50\,\text{m}\) while coming back.
Distance is the total path length:
\[
\text{distance}=50\,\text{m}+50\,\text{m}=100\,\text{m}
\]
For displacement, compare only the final and initial positions.
The runner finishes at the same marker from which the motion started.
\[
\Delta x=0\,\text{m}
\]
A complete return to the starting point makes displacement zero even though the runner has covered a measurable path.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Distance \(=100\,\text{m}\), and displacement \(=0\,\text{m}\).

question: A claim says, “In straight-line motion, distance and displacement must always have the same magnitude.” The claim fails mainly because
opt_a: straight-line motion cannot have a negative coordinate
opt_b: a body can reverse direction while still moving along the same straight line
opt_c: distance is measured in \( \text{s} \), while displacement is measured in \( \text{m} \)
opt_d: displacement is always greater than distance
explanation: Straight-line motion means the motion is confined to one line, not that the body must always move in one direction. If the body reverses direction, the path length already covered still contributes to distance. Displacement, however, depends only on the initial and final positions. In such a case, distance becomes greater than the magnitude of displacement. Both distance and displacement are measured in \( \text{m} \), so the difference is conceptual, not due to different units.

question:
Study the following one-dimensional journey.
PartMotion
P\(x=+1\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+6\,\text{m}\)
Q\(x=+6\,\text{m}\) to \(x=-2\,\text{m}\)
R\(x=-2\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+2\,\text{m}\)
For the whole journey, distance travelled and displacement are respectively
explanation:
\( \textbf{Segment P length:} \)
\[
|+6-(+1)|\,\text{m}=5\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Segment Q length:} \)
\[
|-2-(+6)|\,\text{m}=8\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Segment R length:} \)
\[
|+2-(-2)|\,\text{m}=4\,\text{m}
\]
Total distance is
\[
5\,\text{m}+8\,\text{m}+4\,\text{m}=17\,\text{m}
\]
For displacement, use the first and last coordinates only:
\[
\Delta x=x_{\text{final}}-x_{\text{initial}}=+2\,\text{m}-(+1\,\text{m})
\]
\[
\Delta x=+1\,\text{m}
\]
The intermediate reversal increases distance but does not enter displacement as a separate addition.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Distance \(=17\,\text{m}\), and displacement \(=+1\,\text{m}\).

question:
Assertion: If a body returns to its starting point, its displacement for the complete motion is zero.
Reason: Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The displacement for a complete motion is calculated from final position minus initial position. If the body returns to its starting point, the final position is the same as the initial position. This makes \( \Delta x=0 \), even if the body covered a long route before returning. The Reason states the principle that directly explains the Assertion. Distance would not become zero in general, because distance counts the full path length covered during the journey.

question:
Two paths on the same straight line are described.
Case 1: \(x=0\,\text{m}\rightarrow x=+6\,\text{m}\)
Case 2: \(x=0\,\text{m}\rightarrow x=+4\,\text{m}\rightarrow x=+6\,\text{m}\)
What comparison is valid?
opt_a: Both cases have the same displacement, but Case 2 has greater distance
opt_b: Case 1 has greater displacement, but both have the same distance
opt_c: Case 2 has zero displacement because an intermediate point is used
opt_d: Both cases have the same displacement and the same distance
explanation: In Case 1, the body moves from \(x=0\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+6\,\text{m}\) without reversal, so distance is \(6\,\text{m}\) and displacement is \(+6\,\text{m}\). In Case 2, the body moves from \(x=0\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+4\,\text{m}\), then continues to \(x=+6\,\text{m}\). The distance is \(4\,\text{m}+2\,\text{m}=6\,\text{m}\), and the displacement is still \(+6\,\text{m}\). Passing through an intermediate point does not increase distance unless extra path is covered by reversal or detour. In a straight-line no-reversal journey, distance and displacement magnitude remain equal.

question:
A position graph is described as follows.
An object starts at \(x=0\,\text{m}\), moves steadily to \(x=+4\,\text{m}\), then moves steadily back to \(x=+1\,\text{m}\). The graph is an \(x-t\) graph, but only the sequence of positions is needed here.
What are the distance travelled and displacement?
explanation:
\( \textbf{First part:} \) The object moves from \(x=0\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+4\,\text{m}\), so it covers \(4\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Second part:} \) It then moves back from \(x=+4\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+1\,\text{m}\), so it covers \(3\,\text{m}\).
Thus,
\[
\text{distance}=4\,\text{m}+3\,\text{m}=7\,\text{m}
\]
For displacement,
\[
\Delta x=x_{\text{final}}-x_{\text{initial}}
\]
\[
\Delta x=+1\,\text{m}-0\,\text{m}=+1\,\text{m}
\]
The graph description includes a reversal, so the path length is greater than the net change.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Distance \(=7\,\text{m}\), and displacement \(=+1\,\text{m}\).

question: A body covers a distance of \(18\,\text{m}\) and has displacement \(0\,\text{m}\) during a motion along a straight line. A possible description of the motion is
opt_c: it remains at rest for the whole interval
opt_d: it moves \(9\,\text{m}\) away and stops there
explanation: Zero displacement means the final position is the same as the initial position. A non-zero distance means some path length was actually covered. Moving \(9\,\text{m}\) away and \(9\,\text{m}\) back gives total distance \(18\,\text{m}\) and brings the body back to the starting point. Motion in one direction for \(18\,\text{m}\) would give displacement magnitude \(18\,\text{m}\), not zero. Remaining at rest would give both distance and displacement equal to \(0\,\text{m}\).

question:
The statement pair below refers to straight-line motion.
Statement I: Distance depends on the route actually followed.
Statement II: Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions.
Statement III: Distance can be smaller than \(|\Delta x|\) if the body moves in the negative direction.
explanation: Distance is route-dependent because it adds the length of every part of the path actually travelled. Displacement is position-change dependent because it uses only \(x_2-x_1\). Statement III is false because distance cannot be smaller than the magnitude of displacement. Moving in the negative direction changes the sign of displacement, not the rule \(\text{distance}\geq|\Delta x|\). Direction affects the sign of \(\Delta x\), while distance remains a non-negative path length.

question: A body moves along a line from \(x=-2\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+3\,\text{m}\), then to \(x=-5\,\text{m}\). For this motion, the magnitude of displacement is smaller than the distance because
opt_a: the body changes its direction during the motion
opt_b: the body starts from a negative coordinate
opt_c: the final coordinate is also negative
opt_d: the SI unit of distance is different from that of displacement
explanation: The body first moves from \(x=-2\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+3\,\text{m}\), so it moves toward the positive direction. It then moves from \(x=+3\,\text{m}\) to \(x=-5\,\text{m}\), so it reverses and moves toward the negative direction. Distance adds both path segments. Displacement compares only the final coordinate with the initial coordinate. The smaller magnitude of displacement comes from the reversal, not from starting at a negative coordinate or from any difference in units.

question: Time interval in kinematics is represented by
explanation: A time interval is the elapsed time between two instants. If the first instant is \(t_1\) and the later instant is \(t_2\), the interval is written as \( \Delta t=t_2-t_1 \). The expression \(x_2-x_1\) represents change in position, not time interval. The expression \(v_2-v_1\) represents change in velocity. Average quantities such as average speed and average velocity need a time interval, so the order of subtraction matters.

question: A stopwatch reads \(3\,\text{s}\) when a cart starts being observed and \(11\,\text{s}\) when the observation ends. The time interval is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial time reading:} \) \(t_1=3\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Final time reading:} \) \(t_2=11\,\text{s}\).
The time interval is the elapsed time:
\[
\Delta t=t_2-t_1
\]
\[
\Delta t=11\,\text{s}-3\,\text{s}
\]
\[
\Delta t=8\,\text{s}
\]
The starting reading \(3\,\text{s}\) is not the duration of the observation.
The duration is found from the difference between the two readings.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The time interval is \(8\,\text{s}\).

question: In the expression \(v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\), the symbol \(\Delta t\) should represent
opt_a: a single instant at which the object is located
opt_b: the final position coordinate of the object
opt_c: the elapsed time between two position readings
opt_d: the total distance covered by the object
explanation: Average velocity compares displacement with the time interval over which that displacement occurs. The symbol \(\Delta t\) means the difference between final and initial time readings, \(t_2-t_1\). A single instant such as \(t=5\,\text{s}\) is not enough to define an average over an interval. The final position coordinate belongs to \(x\), not to \(\Delta t\). Confusing an instant with an interval can lead to using the wrong denominator in average-quantity calculations.

question: An object is photographed at \(t=2\,\text{s}\), \(t=5\,\text{s}\), and \(t=9\,\text{s}\). The interval from the first photograph to the last photograph is
explanation:
\( \textbf{First photograph:} \) \(t_1=2\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Last photograph:} \) \(t_2=9\,\text{s}\).
The intermediate photograph at \(t=5\,\text{s}\) does not change the total interval from first to last.
\[
\Delta t=t_2-t_1
\]
\[
\Delta t=9\,\text{s}-2\,\text{s}
\]
\[
\Delta t=7\,\text{s}
\]
Time interval is an elapsed duration, not the sum of all time readings.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The interval from first to last photograph is \(7\,\text{s}\).

question: Average speed for a complete journey is found by using
opt_a: total displacement divided by total time
opt_b: final position divided by total time
opt_c: change in velocity divided by time interval
opt_d: total distance divided by total time
explanation: Average speed describes how fast the total path has been covered during a whole journey. It uses total distance travelled, not displacement, because speed is related to path length. It is a scalar quantity, so it does not carry a positive or negative sign. The time used must be the total time taken for the same journey. Change in velocity divided by time belongs to acceleration, not average speed.

question: A cyclist covers \(180\,\text{m}\) in \(12\,\text{s}\). The average speed is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Total distance \(=180\,\text{m}\), total time \(=12\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Average speed.
Average speed is defined as
\[
v_{\text{avg speed}}=\frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}
\]
This relation applies because speed uses path length covered per unit time.
Substituting the values,
\[
v_{\text{avg speed}}=\frac{180\,\text{m}}{12\,\text{s}}
\]
\[
v_{\text{avg speed}}=15\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The unit becomes \( \text{m s}^{-1} \) because metre is divided by second.
No direction sign is attached because average speed is scalar.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The average speed is \(15\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: A car moves at \(10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) for \(4\,\text{s}\) and then at \(20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) for \(6\,\text{s}\) along the same road. Its average speed for the whole trip is
explanation:
\( \textbf{First part:} \) Speed \(=10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), time \(=4\,\text{s}\).
\[
\text{Distance in first part}=10\times4=40\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Second part:} \) Speed \(=20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), time \(=6\,\text{s}\).
\[
\text{Distance in second part}=20\times6=120\,\text{m}
\]
Total distance is
\[
40\,\text{m}+120\,\text{m}=160\,\text{m}
\]
Total time is
\[
4\,\text{s}+6\,\text{s}=10\,\text{s}
\]
Average speed is
\[
v_{\text{avg speed}}=\frac{160\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{s}}=16\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The arithmetic mean \(15\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) is not valid here because the two speeds are not maintained for equal times.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The average speed is \(16\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: A runner covers the first \(100\,\text{m}\) at \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and the next \(100\,\text{m}\) at \(10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). What is the average speed for the \(200\,\text{m}\) run?
explanation:
\( \textbf{First distance:} \) \(100\,\text{m}\) at \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\[
t_1=\frac{100\,\text{m}}{5\,\text{m s}^{-1}}=20\,\text{s}
\]
\( \textbf{Second distance:} \) \(100\,\text{m}\) at \(10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\[
t_2=\frac{100\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{m s}^{-1}}=10\,\text{s}
\]
Total distance is
\[
100\,\text{m}+100\,\text{m}=200\,\text{m}
\]
Total time is
\[
20\,\text{s}+10\,\text{s}=30\,\text{s}
\]
Average speed is
\[
v_{\text{avg speed}}=\frac{200\,\text{m}}{30\,\text{s}}=6.67\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The value is not \(7.50\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) because equal distances do not make the arithmetic mean of speeds valid.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The average speed is \(6.67\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question:

question: A train covers \(72\,\text{km}\) in \(1\,\text{h}\). Its average speed in SI units is
explanation:

v_{\text{avg speed}}=20\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The value \(72\) belongs to \( \text{km h}^{-1} \), not to \( \text{m s}^{-1} \).

question: A traveller moves for equal time intervals: \(8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) for \(5\,\text{s}\) and \(12\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) for \(5\,\text{s}\). Why does the average speed equal the arithmetic mean of the two speeds in this case?
opt_a: Because the distances in the two parts are equal
opt_b: Because the direction of motion is ignored in all physics quantities
opt_c: Because average speed is always the arithmetic mean of speeds
opt_d: Because the two time intervals are equal
explanation: Average speed is total distance divided by total time. When two different speeds act for equal time intervals, the distance contribution of each speed is proportional to that speed for the same duration. For this case, the total distance is \(8\times5+12\times5=100\,\text{m}\), and the total time is \(10\,\text{s}\). The average speed is therefore \(10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), which is the arithmetic mean of \(8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(12\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). This shortcut depends on equal times and should not be used for unequal time intervals or equal-distance cases.

question: The following statement is made about a two-part trip: “The average speed is the average of the two speed readings.” The statement is safe only when
opt_a: the two parts take equal times
opt_b: the two parts cover equal distances
opt_d: the motion is along the negative direction
explanation: Average speed is based on total distance divided by total time, so each part must be weighted according to how long the body moves at that speed. If the time intervals are equal, the arithmetic mean of the two speeds gives the same result as the total-distance over total-time calculation. If the distances are equal, the slower part takes more time and the arithmetic mean is generally wrong. Direction does not affect speed because speed is scalar, but it does not justify the arithmetic-mean shortcut. The condition of equal time intervals is what makes the simple average valid.

question: Average velocity in one-dimensional motion is calculated from
opt_a: total distance divided by total time
opt_c: final speed divided by initial speed
opt_d: path length multiplied by time interval
explanation: Average velocity describes the rate of net change of position over a time interval. In one dimension, it is written as \(v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\). Since \(\Delta x\) can be positive, negative, or zero, average velocity can also carry a sign. Total distance divided by total time gives average speed, not average velocity. The distinction matters most when the body reverses direction or returns to its starting point.

question: A particle moves from \(x=-4\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+8\,\text{m}\) in \(6\,\text{s}\). Its average velocity is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial position:} \) \(x_1=-4\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final position:} \) \(x_2=+8\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Time interval:} \) \(\Delta t=6\,\text{s}\).
Displacement is
\[
\Delta x=x_2-x_1
\]
\[
\Delta x=+8\,\text{m}-(-4\,\text{m})=+12\,\text{m}
\]
Average velocity is
\[
v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}
\]
\[
v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{+12\,\text{m}}{6\,\text{s}}=+2\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The positive sign shows that the net change of position is in the positive direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The average velocity is \(+2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: A moving object starts at \(x=+10\,\text{m}\), reaches \(x=+2\,\text{m}\) after \(4\,\text{s}\), and does not need any distance data for this question. Its average velocity is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial coordinate:} \) \(x_1=+10\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Final coordinate:} \) \(x_2=+2\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Time interval:} \) \(\Delta t=4\,\text{s}\).
Displacement is
\[
\Delta x=x_2-x_1=+2\,\text{m}-(+10\,\text{m})
\]
\[
\Delta x=-8\,\text{m}
\]
Average velocity is
\[
v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{-8\,\text{m}}{4\,\text{s}}
\]
\[
v_{\text{avg}}=-2\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The negative sign comes from the decreasing position coordinate.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The average velocity is \(-2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: A boy runs from a starting point to a wall \(30\,\text{m}\) away and then returns to the starting point in a total time of \(20\,\text{s}\). His average velocity for the complete motion is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Path covered:} \) The boy runs \(30\,\text{m}\) to the wall and \(30\,\text{m}\) back.
For average velocity, the path length is not the numerator.
The boy starts and ends at the same point.
So the displacement for the complete motion is
\[
\Delta x=0\,\text{m}
\]
Average velocity is
\[
v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}
\]
\[
v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{0\,\text{m}}{20\,\text{s}}=0\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The distance is \(60\,\text{m}\), so average speed would not be zero.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The average velocity is \(0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question:

The calculation needs both the change in position and the elapsed time.

question:

A cart moves on a straight line. It starts at \(x=0\,\text{m}\), goes to \(x=+12\,\text{m}\), then comes back and stops at \(x=+4\,\text{m}\). The whole motion takes \(8\,\text{s}\).
The average velocity for the whole motion is
explanation:

\]
The total time interval is

\]
Average velocity is

\]
Using \(20\,\text{m}\) as the numerator would calculate average speed, not average velocity.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The average velocity is \(+0.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question:
Consider the following statements.
Statement I: Average speed is always non-negative.
Statement II: Average velocity can be negative in one-dimensional motion.
Statement III: Average velocity uses total distance as its numerator.
explanation: Average speed is based on total distance, and distance is non-negative. Average velocity is based on displacement, which can be positive, negative, or zero in one-dimensional motion. Therefore, average velocity can be negative if the final position lies in the negative direction from the initial position. Statement III is false because total distance belongs to average speed. Mixing the two numerators is the usual reason for getting the same value for average speed and average velocity in a reversal problem.

question:

explanation: Average speed uses total distance as its numerator. Average velocity uses displacement, written as \(\Delta x\). In a round trip, the final position equals the initial position, so the displacement and hence the numerator for average velocity is \(0\). Average speed in a round trip still uses the total path length covered, which is generally non-zero. This matching keeps the scalar path-length idea separate from the signed displacement idea.

question: A car moves \(100\,\text{m}\) east in \(10\,\text{s}\), then \(60\,\text{m}\) west in \(5\,\text{s}\). Taking east as positive, its average velocity for the whole motion is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Sign convention:} \) East is positive.
\( \textbf{First displacement:} \) \(+100\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Second displacement:} \) West is negative, so it is \(-60\,\text{m}\).
Net displacement is
\[
\Delta x=+100\,\text{m}-60\,\text{m}=+40\,\text{m}
\]
Total time is
\[
\Delta t=10\,\text{s}+5\,\text{s}=15\,\text{s}
\]
Average velocity is
\[
v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}
\]
\[
v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{+40\,\text{m}}{15\,\text{s}}=+2.67\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The total distance \(160\,\text{m}\) would give average speed, not average velocity.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The average velocity is \(+2.67\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: In a straight-line trip, the average speed and the magnitude of average velocity will be equal if the body
opt_c: spends equal times in opposite directions
opt_d: has negative displacement during the interval
explanation: Average speed is \(\frac{\text{total distance}}{\Delta t}\), while the magnitude of average velocity is \(\frac{|\Delta x|}{\Delta t}\). These two are equal when total distance equals \(|\Delta x|\). In one-dimensional motion, that equality occurs when the body does not reverse direction during the interval. If the body returns to the starting point, \(|\Delta x|=0\) while distance may be non-zero. A negative displacement only tells the direction of net change and does not prevent equality if the motion stays in one direction.

question: A cart travels from \(x=0\,\text{m}\) to \(x=+20\,\text{m}\) and returns to \(x=+5\,\text{m}\) in \(10\,\text{s}\). What are its average speed and average velocity for the whole motion?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Path details:} \) The cart moves from \(0\,\text{m}\) to \(+20\,\text{m}\), then back to \(+5\,\text{m}\).
First path length:
\[
20\,\text{m}
\]
Return path length:
\[
|+5-(+20)|\,\text{m}=15\,\text{m}
\]
Total distance is
\[
20\,\text{m}+15\,\text{m}=35\,\text{m}
\]
Average speed is
\[
\frac{35\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{s}}=3.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
Displacement is
\[
\Delta x=+5\,\text{m}-0\,\text{m}=+5\,\text{m}
\]
Average velocity is
\[
v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{+5\,\text{m}}{10\,\text{s}}=+0.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The reversal makes total distance much larger than the magnitude of displacement.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Average speed \(=3.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), and average velocity \(=+0.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: A body has average speed \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and average velocity \(-2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) during a time interval. This combination means that the body
opt_a: average speed \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), net displacement negative
opt_b: average speed \(-2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), net displacement positive
explanation: Average speed depends on total distance divided by total time, so it is never negative. Average velocity depends on displacement divided by time interval, so it can be positive, negative, or zero. A negative average velocity means the final position lies in the negative direction from the initial position. The body may still have covered a larger total path length during the same interval. The two values are not contradictory because one describes total path covered and the other describes net change in position.

question:

\]

Average speed is

\]
The westward part reduces displacement but still adds to distance.

question:
Consider the following statements about average speed and average velocity.
Statement I: Average speed cannot be negative.
Statement II: The magnitude of average velocity can never exceed average speed for the same time interval.
Statement III: Average speed and average velocity always have the same magnitude in one-dimensional motion.
explanation: Average speed is based on total distance, so it cannot be negative. The magnitude of average velocity is \(\frac{|\Delta x|}{\Delta t}\), while average speed is \(\frac{\text{distance}}{\Delta t}\). Since \(\text{distance}\geq|\Delta x|\), the magnitude of average velocity cannot be greater than average speed for the same time interval. Statement III is false because reversal can make distance greater than displacement magnitude. The two magnitudes become equal only when the motion has no reversal during the interval.

question: A body returns to its starting point after covering \(120\,\text{m}\) in \(40\,\text{s}\). The average speed and average velocity are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Total distance:} \) \(120\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Total time:} \) \(40\,\text{s}\).
Average speed is
\[
\frac{120\,\text{m}}{40\,\text{s}}=3\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The body returns to its starting point, so the final position equals the initial position.
Thus displacement is
\[
\Delta x=0\,\text{m}
\]
Average velocity is
\[
v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{0\,\text{m}}{40\,\text{s}}=0\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
A non-zero path length can coexist with zero net change in position.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Average speed \(=3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), and average velocity \(=0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: A straight-line journey has average speed equal to the magnitude of average velocity. A reasonable conclusion is that during the interval the body
opt_a: did not reverse its direction of motion
opt_d: had zero displacement and non-zero distance
explanation: Average speed and the magnitude of average velocity have the same denominator, the total time interval. Their equality requires the total distance to equal the magnitude of displacement. In one-dimensional motion, this happens when the body moves along the line without reversal between the initial and final positions. If the body returns to the starting point, displacement is zero while distance may be non-zero. Equality here is a statement about path shape and direction change, not about rest.

question:

explanation:

v_{\text{avg}}=\frac{-8\,\text{m}}{4\,\text{s}}=-2\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
The negative sign belongs to average velocity because displacement is signed.
Average speed remains positive because distance is path length.
The two calculations use the same time interval but different numerators.

question: A body moves with constant velocity when it
opt_a: equal distances with direction change each interval
opt_b: increasing speed in every equal time interval
opt_c: zero position coordinate at every instant
opt_d: equal signed displacements in equal time intervals
explanation: Constant velocity means both magnitude and direction of velocity remain unchanged. In one-dimensional motion, this is shown by equal displacements in equal time intervals with the same sign of displacement each time. Merely covering equal distances is not enough if the direction keeps changing. Increasing speed would indicate non-uniform motion, not constant velocity. The body can have constant velocity at any position; it does not need to stay at \(x=0\,\text{m}\).

question: A train moving along a straight track has constant velocity \(+12\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). How much displacement does it have in \(5\,\text{s}\)?
explanation:

\[

\]
The relation applies because the velocity does not change during the interval.
Substituting the values,
\[
s=(+12\,\text{m s}^{-1})(5\,\text{s})
\]

s=+60\,\text{m}
\]
The positive sign shows displacement in the chosen positive direction.
The unit reduces to \( \text{m} \) because \( \text{s}^{-1} \) and \( \text{s} \) cancel.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The displacement is \(+60\,\text{m}\).

question: In uniform motion with constant velocity \(v\), the position at time \(t\) is represented by \(x=x_0+vt\). The term \(x_0\) represents
explanation: In the equation \(x=x_0+vt\), \(x\) is the position at time \(t\). The symbol \(x_0\) represents the initial position, commonly the position at \(t=0\). The term \(vt\) gives the displacement during time \(t\) when velocity is constant. Acceleration does not appear in this equation because constant velocity means acceleration is zero. The equation describes signed position on the chosen line, not total distance in a back-and-forth path.

question: A cart is at \(x_0=-3\,\text{m}\) at \(t=0\,\text{s}\) and moves with constant velocity \(+2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). Its position at \(t=6\,\text{s}\) is
explanation:

The positive final coordinate means the cart has crossed the origin and is now on the positive side.

question: The \(x-t\) graph of a body is a straight line with positive slope. This graph represents
opt_b: uniform motion in the positive direction
opt_c: increasing acceleration in the positive direction
opt_d: motion with velocity changing sign repeatedly
explanation: On an \(x-t\) graph, slope represents velocity. A straight line has constant slope, so it represents constant velocity. If the slope is positive, the position coordinate increases with time, so the motion is in the positive direction. A horizontal line would represent rest because its slope is zero. A changing acceleration or repeatedly changing velocity would require a graph whose slope does not remain constant.

question:

TimePosition

explanation:

\[
v=\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}

\[

question: A horizontal line on an \(x-t\) graph means that the body
opt_c: is at rest in the chosen frame
explanation: On an \(x-t\) graph, the slope gives velocity. A horizontal line has zero slope because the position coordinate remains constant as time changes. Therefore, the velocity is \(0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) in the chosen frame. This means the body is at rest relative to that frame. A non-zero constant velocity would produce a sloping straight line, not a horizontal one.

question: A motion has position equation \(x=5-3t\), where \(x\) is in \( \text{m} \) and \(t\) is in \( \text{s} \). The motion is best described as
opt_d: uniformly accelerated motion with acceleration \(-3\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)
explanation:
The standard constant-velocity form is
\[
x=x_0+vt
\]
The given equation is
\[
x=5-3t
\]
Comparing the two equations, the initial position is
\[
x_0=5\,\text{m}
\]
The coefficient of \(t\) is the velocity:
\[
v=-3\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
Since the coefficient of \(t\) is constant, the velocity is constant.
The negative sign means the position coordinate decreases with time.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The body has uniform motion with velocity \(-3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: A car covers equal displacements of \(15\,\text{m}\) in every \(3\,\text{s}\) interval along the same direction. Its acceleration is
explanation:
Equal displacements in equal time intervals along the same direction indicate constant velocity. The velocity in each interval is
\[
v=\frac{15\,\text{m}}{3\,\text{s}}=5\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
Since this velocity does not change from one interval to the next, the change in velocity is zero.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
So,
\[
a=0\,\text{m s}^{-2}
\]
The value \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) is velocity, not acceleration.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The acceleration is \(0\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).

question:
Assertion: A body moving with constant velocity has zero acceleration.
Reason: Acceleration measures the rate of change of velocity with time.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: Constant velocity means that velocity does not change with time. Acceleration is connected with change in velocity per unit time. If the change in velocity is zero over every time interval, the acceleration is \(0\,\text{m s}^{-2}\). The Reason states the exact principle used to understand the Assertion. This remains true even if the constant velocity is negative, because negative constant velocity still has no change in velocity.

question: For a body obeying \(x=x_0+vt\), doubling the time interval while keeping \(v\) constant will double
explanation: For constant velocity, displacement during time \(t\) is \(s=vt\). If \(v\) remains constant, displacement is directly proportional to time. Doubling \(t\) changes \(vt\) to \(v(2t)=2vt\), so the displacement doubles. The initial position \(x_0\) is fixed by where the body was at \(t=0\,\text{s}\). Acceleration remains zero for constant velocity, and units do not change when the time interval is changed.

question: A straight-line \(x-t\) graph has a constant negative slope. The motion represented is
opt_b: uniform motion in the negative direction
opt_d: motion with zero displacement in every interval
explanation: On an \(x-t\) graph, the slope gives velocity. A straight line has constant slope, so the velocity is constant. If the slope is negative, the position coordinate decreases with time. This means the body moves in the negative direction with uniform velocity. A horizontal line would represent rest, while a curved graph would show changing velocity.

question: A body follows \(x=12-4t\), where \(x\) is in \( \text{m} \) and \(t\) is in \( \text{s} \). Its displacement from \(t=1\,\text{s}\) to \(t=4\,\text{s}\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Position function:} \)
\[
x=12-4t
\]
At \(t=1\,\text{s}\),
\[
x_1=12-4(1)=8\,\text{m}
\]
At \(t=4\,\text{s}\),
\[
x_2=12-4(4)=-4\,\text{m}
\]
Displacement is
\[
\Delta x=x_2-x_1
\]
\[
\Delta x=-4\,\text{m}-8\,\text{m}
\]
\[
\Delta x=-12\,\text{m}
\]
The negative sign matches the negative constant velocity in the equation.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The displacement is \(-12\,\text{m}\).

question: For a body moving with constant velocity, displacement is directly proportional to time because
opt_b: distance is always equal to zero
opt_c: velocity remains fixed while time changes
opt_d: the origin moves with the body
explanation: For constant velocity, the displacement in time \(t\) is given by \(s=vt\). If \(v\) remains fixed, then \(s\) changes in the same ratio as \(t\). For example, doubling the time doubles the displacement, provided the velocity is unchanged. This proportionality does not require acceleration; in fact, acceleration is zero for constant velocity. The origin is only a reference point and does not cause the proportional relation.

question:
Study the position table for a moving object.
TimePosition
\(0\,\text{s}\)\(18\,\text{m}\)
\(2\,\text{s}\)\(12\,\text{m}\)
\(4\,\text{s}\)\(6\,\text{m}\)
\(6\,\text{s}\)\(0\,\text{m}\)
The motion is best described as
opt_c: non-uniform motion with increasing positive velocity
explanation:
In each \(2\,\text{s}\) interval, the position decreases by \(6\,\text{m}\). Equal displacements occur in equal time intervals, so the velocity is constant. The velocity is
\[
v=\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}
\]
\[
v=\frac{-6\,\text{m}}{2\,\text{s}}=-3\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
